I think that one of the reasons retro JRPGs are so popular is because they didn't have voice acting. If you don't have to pay for recording/voice actors, there can be significantly more dialogue between characters, which makes their relationships feel more meaningful. It also means that characters sound like whatever the player imagines they sound like. More than once I've had a character ruined for me because their voice doesn't mesh with their personality/aesthetic.

I agree, certainly for RPGs with a lot of text. Final Fantasy games before 10 were better then after because of voice acting. I gave up on 10 when the two main characters (Tidus and Yuna, was it) are laughing or shouting over some cliff. The two Trails games I've played lacked voice acting (though there were still grunts and similar in battle) and were very compelling. Defenders Quest (a tower defence and RPG blend) doesn't have voice acting and manages to convey humour with static cartoons and text. It certainly is not necessary.

Often, I don't like the American voices used, especially if they use a Texas or other Southern accent as a substitute for that Japanese dialect/accent. A double-whammy is if the translation still uses a lot of Japanese words (proper nouns) and then hearing people make a pig's ear pronouncing them. These are actual downsides to having voice active. Now when I'm buying a JRPG I look to see if it comes with the Jap voices and English text. I should consider looking for other audio when I buy a Western RPG.
